items.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram

solutionCode.label: the POP reveals the width; sentinels remove every edge case
solutionCode.py:
def largest_rectangle_area(heights: list) -> int:
    h = list(heights) + [0]        # SENTINEL: forces the stack to fully drain
    st = []                        # indices, increasing height
    best = 0
    for i, cur in enumerate(h):
        while st and h[st[-1]] >= cur:
            height = h[st.pop()]
            # left boundary is the new top (EXCLUSIVE), right is i (EXCLUSIVE)
            left = st[-1] if st else -1
            best = max(best, height * (i - left - 1))
        st.append(i)
    return best

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each bar is pushed and popped exactly once. Space O(n).

followups.a: Push 0 (h=2). At i=1 (h=1) pop index 0: height 2, left=-1, width 1-(-1)-1=1, area 2. Push 1. Push 2 (h=5), push 3 (h=6). At i=4 (h=2) pop 3: height 6, left=2, width 4-2-1=1, area 6. Pop 2: height 5, left=1, width 4-1-1=2, area 10 — the answer. Then push 4, push 5, and the sentinel drains the rest.

followups.q: Why is the width i - left - 1 and not i - left?
followups.a: Both boundaries are EXCLUSIVE: index left holds a strictly shorter bar and index i holds a shorter-or-equal bar, so neither is part of the rectangle. The bars actually spanned are left+1 through i-1, which is i - left - 1 of them. Using i - left overcounts by one on every rectangle.

items.title: Maximal Rectangle
items.statement: Binary matrix biggest 1-rectangle via row-histograms + K301.
hints: Call solver per row; track global best.

solutionCode.label: each row is a histogram; reuse the K301 solver

items.complexity: Time O(rows * cols) — one O(cols) histogram solve per row. Space O(cols).

followups.q: Why must a zero reset the height to 0 rather than decrement it?
followups.a: heights[j] means "how many consecutive 1s end at this row in column j". A zero breaks the run entirely, so the count restarts from nothing. Decrementing would claim a column of 1s that is not contiguous, and the histogram would describe a rectangle that does not exist in the matrix.

followups.q: Why is this O(rows * cols) and not O(rows * cols^2)?
followups.a: Building each row histogram is O(cols), and the histogram solver is O(cols) because of the push-once pop-once amortisation. So each row costs O(cols) and there are rows of them. The reduction is what turns a 2D search into a stack of 1D ones.

items.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
items.statement: Section flagship; then O(1)-space two-pass counter variant.

solutionCode.label: index-base barrier on the stack, plus the O(1)-space two-pass counter

items.complexity: Stack version: O(n) time, O(n) space. Two-pass counter version: O(n) time, O(1) space.

followups.q: What is the -1 barrier actually doing?
followups.a: It is the index just before the current valid run, so i - st.top() gives the run length directly. Without it you would need a separate "start of run" variable and a branch for the first match. When an unmatched ")" appears it replaces the barrier, because no valid run can span past it.

followups.q: Why does the O(1) version need TWO passes?
followups.a: The left-to-right counter resets when closers exceed openers, so it correctly handles ")(" but never detects a run that ends with surplus openers — "(()" leaves open=2, close=1 and it never fires. Scanning right to left catches exactly that case. Neither direction alone is complete.

items.title: Asteroid Collision
hints: while enemy-on-top loop; equal sizes annihilate pair.

solutionCode.label: collisions happen only when a right-mover meets a left-mover

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once. Space O(n).

followups.a: Only a positive (moving right) followed by a negative (moving left) — they converge. Negative then positive diverge, and same-sign pairs travel together forever. That single condition, `x < 0 and st[-1] > 0`, is the whole physics of the problem.

followups.q: Why does the equal-size case pop but still kill x?
followups.a: Equal sizes annihilate both. The pop removes the stack asteroid and setting alive=false discards x, so neither is pushed. Popping without clearing alive would let x survive and continue colliding — a common off-by-one-asteroid bug.

items.title: Remove K Digits

solutionCode.label: greedily pop any digit larger than its successor

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each digit is pushed and popped at most once. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why does removing a left-side peak always help?
followups.a: Digit position dominates digit value: any digit further left contributes more to the number's magnitude. If a digit is larger than the one after it, deleting it lets every following digit shift one place left and lowers the leading digit — a strict improvement. Greedy is exact here because that argument holds at every step.

followups.q: Why the two cleanup steps at the end?
followups.a: If the input is non-decreasing ("12345") nothing is ever popped in the loop, so the remaining budget must come off the tail — the least significant digits. And "10200" with k=1 yields "0200", which is not a valid number, so leading zeros are stripped and an empty result becomes "0".

items.title: Decode String

solutionCode.label: two stacks: one for repeat counts, one for the prefix built so far

items.complexity: Time O(total output length), space O(nesting depth * segment length).

followups.q: Why does the number need num = num*10 + d?
followups.a: Counts can exceed 9. Reading "12[a]" digit by digit without accumulation gives 1 then 2, producing "aa" instead of twelve a's. The accumulator is what makes multi-digit repeat counts work, and LeetCode tests exactly that.

followups.q: Why two stacks rather than one stack of pairs?
followups.a: They are pushed and popped in lockstep, so a single stack of (count, prefix) pairs is equally correct and arguably cleaner. Two stacks mirror the C++ types more directly. What matters is that both values are saved at "[" and restored at "]" — losing the prefix is what breaks nested cases like "3[a2[c]]".

items.title: Next Smaller Element family
items.statement: NSE left/right variants; note strict vs non-strict consequences for duplicates.
hints: Tie handling decides later contribution formulas.

solutionCode.label: one skeleton, four variants: flip the direction and the strictness
solutionCode.py:
def next_smaller_right(a: list) -> list:
    """NEXT smaller to the RIGHT (strict). Pop while top is GREATER than current."""
    n = len(a)
    out = [-1] * n
    st = []
    for i, cur in enumerate(a):
        while st and a[st[-1]] > cur:
            out[st.pop()] = cur
        st.append(i)
    return out


def prev_smaller_left(a: list) -> list:
    """PREVIOUS smaller to the LEFT (strict). Read the surviving top."""
    n = len(a)
    out = [-1] * n
    st = []
    for i, cur in enumerate(a):
        while st and a[st[-1]] >= cur:
            st.pop()
        out[i] = a[st[-1]] if st else -1
        st.append(i)
    return out


def next_smaller_or_equal_right(a: list) -> list:
    """NON-STRICT: >= instead of > changes who wins a TIE.

    Ties matter: for contribution counting exactly ONE side must be non-strict,
    or equal elements double-count the spans between them."""
    n = len(a)
    out = [-1] * n
    st = []
    for i, cur in enumerate(a):
        while st and a[st[-1]] >= cur:
            out[st.pop()] = cur
        st.append(i)
    return out

items.complexity: All four variants are O(n) time and O(n) space.

followups.q: What changes between "next greater" and "next smaller"?
followups.a: One comparison operator. Greater keeps a decreasing stack and pops on a larger arrival; smaller keeps an increasing stack and pops on a smaller arrival. Direction (previous versus next) is the other axis: previous reads the surviving top after popping, next writes to the popped index.

followups.q: Why does tie handling decide the contribution formula?
followups.a: For a duplicated minimum, a subarray containing both copies would be counted once for each if both boundaries were strict — double counting. Making exactly one side non-strict assigns every such subarray to precisely one copy. Which side you relax is arbitrary; relaxing both or neither is wrong.
